rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-IV, Table V - the authors implemented SWARM on a 250 ft x 80 ft groundnut farm in Kuppam, Andhra Pradesh, tested it for about 1.5 months and tabulated results. Q2: Table V and Conclusion - the sensor-driven software-controlled system applied 490 mm water versus 540 mm under manual irrigation against an exact requirement of 420 mm; manual supplied 129% of requirement and SWARM 117%, a direct 12% wastage avoided; urea 37.8 kg vs 39 kg. Q8: Section III.B and II.A - the authors state they could not obtain the SPAD chlorophyll sensor and substituted twice-daily lab leaf measurements keyed in manually, could not obtain satellite images and used a sample image, and the trial covered only about 1.5 months (data to 11 April, system still running).
rows.notes: Single farm, single crop (groundnut), single season; water saving is a single comparison of applied water with no replication, no dispersion statistics and no reported soil-moisture or drainage data as intermediate variable (moisture meters were used as control input but no soil water results are reported). Scale is a ~0.46 ha farm divided into two sections, i.e. a single field. Conditions mentioned (low cost, simple interface for uneducated farmers, crop-stage sensitivity) are design considerations, not stated requirements for the saving.

notes: Conference paper with OCR noise in Table IV and the future research section; results table (Table V) is legible. The claim passage is a general statement about real-time monitoring optimizing resource use; the study's own result is a single-farm comparison of water and urea applied by SWARM versus manual practice.
